messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amara was twenty years old when it happened, working the late shift at a high-end restaurant in Atlanta where he was a line chef. He had come to the United States from Ghana three years earlier, driven by a fierce ambition to build something for himself. That night, after closing, three men cornered him in the alley behind the kitchen. He remembered the sound of a car backfiring somewhere down the street just before they grabbed him. He remembered the violence of it, the way his body was used, the absolute absence of any choice. He did not fight back. He froze. And in the months that followed, that freezing became the thing he could not forgive himself for.

Amara now lives in a state of constant, low-grade alarm. He reacts as if he is in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, his heart hammering at a sudden movement from a coworker reaching for a pan. He feels on guard even inside his own apartment, and he cannot relax. Car sounds—a backfire, a loud exhaust, even a door slamming—can instantly bring the full memory back without warning. When that happens, he sometimes hears things in his head that he heard that night, fragments of voices or the scrape of shoes on concrete, and the memory crashes into him so completely that he loses the thread of whatever he was doing. He has come to believe that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, that he acted in ways that go against who he is, and that he has no future. These beliefs make the world feel full of potential threats, and they also make the memories more frequent; when he feels worthless, he finds himself revisiting the alley again and again, as if trying to rewrite it.

His maladaptive strategies have become a daily ritual. He constantly checks his body for signs of danger or injury, scanning his arms and torso for bruises or marks that might indicate he has been harmed without realizing it. He detaches himself from the memories when they surface, mentally stepping out of his own head, but this detachment only seems to make the memories more intrusive later. The revenge fantasies are the most consuming. He imagines getting revenge on the people responsible, running through elaborate scenarios in which he is no longer the one who froze. These fantasies give him a fleeting sense of control, but they also feed his negative appraisals—because a person who dreams of violence must be a bad person, and that confirms that he acted in ways that go against who he is. The fantasies also make the memories worse, because the imagined violence mirrors the real violence, and the line between what happened and what he wishes he had done begins to blur.

The cycle is tight and self-reinforcing. A loud car on his walk to work triggers a memory, which triggers a surge of threat, which triggers body-checking and revenge fantasies, which trigger more negative appraisals, which make the next trigger more potent. He has started leaving work early when the kitchen gets too loud, claiming illness. His manager has noticed. His tip share has dropped. He is losing money and credibility, and he is certain he has no future. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week when a delivery truck backfired outside the restaurant and he dropped a full tray of plates, shattering them in front of the head chef. He stood there, frozen, just as he had in the alley, and he realized he could not keep living like this. He is afraid that talking about it will make the memories worse, but he is more afraid of what will happen if he does not.
